passage.title: Green Space as Urban Infrastructure
passage.subtitle: Why cities are budgeting for parks the way they budget for drains

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Urban green space has moved from being a decorative afterthought to a measurable component of city planning. Municipal engineers now treat parks the way they treat drainage: as infrastructure with a maintenance budget and a performance target.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most cited benefit is temperature regulation. Measurements across twelve European cities found that neighbourhoods with continuous tree canopy were up to four degrees cooler during heat waves than districts of comparable density without one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second benefit concerns water. Vegetated surfaces absorb rainfall that would otherwise overwhelm combined sewers, which reduces the frequency of overflow events. Engineers describe this as attenuating the peak flow rather than increasing total capacity.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not all schemes perform equally, however. A review of forty regeneration projects concluded that parks created without a long-term maintenance commitment frequently deteriorated within a decade, and in several cases were perceived as less safe than the sites they replaced.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Planners have drawn a practical lesson from these mixed results. Green space delivers the benefits described above only when funding for upkeep is committed at the same time as the capital works, and when local residents are consulted about how the space will actually be used. Where both conditions hold, the infrastructure analogy appears to be justified.
